prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I would have come. When you called. But. I had the most beautiful pale pink rose. Its healthy stem was clenched between my teeth. And. Its thorns bit sharply into my tender wet flesh. So. I couldn't answer you. Still. My lips moved at you silently. They offered words you never heard. They screamed inside my crazed brain. Only. It could do nothing for you. In time the petals wilted. They blew away. And. They became compost in someone else's garden. The tough, fibrous stem withered. I bit down hard to snap its grip on me. Then. My teeth fell out. Its thorns had burrowed into my cheeks. They had implanted themselves permanently. They were suckling on my softest tissues. And. Not long after they sprouted tiny shoots. They coiled their way down. I still held the memory of your call. And. The long stemmed beauty lodged next to it. They cleaved unto the long roots curling down my neck. My body held tight and listened. Hard.

Here are a few ways to polish your text, elevating the prose into eloquent, literary language while preserving all of your striking, visceral imagery.

### Option 1: Lyrical & Flowing (Recommended)
> I would have answered when you called. Yet, clenched between my teeth was the stem of an exquisite, pale pink rose, its sharp thorns piercing the tender flesh of my mouth and rendering me silent. Still, my lips moved without sound, shaping words you would never hear—screams trapped within a frantic mind, powerless to reach you.
>
> In time, the petals wilted and blew away, becoming nourishment for someone else’s garden. When the tough, fibrous stem hardened, I bit down to break its hold, only for my teeth to give way. The thorns had already burrowed permanently into my cheeks, drawing life from my softest tissues. Soon after, tiny shoots sprouted, coiling their way downward. 
> 
> Entwined with the long roots curling down my neck, the memory of your call remained, forever bound to the long-stemmed beauty. Silent and unyielding, my body held fast and listened. 

---

### Option 2: Dark Gothic & Dramatic
> I would have come at your call. But I was bound by a pale pink rose of breathtaking beauty, its vibrant stem gripped tightly between my teeth, its thorns biting deep into the tender flesh of my mouth. I could not answer. Even so, my lips moved silently, offering words that never reached your ears while my tormented mind screamed inside. Yet, it offered you no aid.
>
> Eventually, the petals withered and swept away, turning to compost in a stranger's garden. As the tough, fibrous stem hardened, I bit down fiercely to shatter its grip, only to lose my teeth in the effort. The thorns had already embedded themselves permanently, feeding upon my softest tissue. Before long, delicate shoots sprouted and coiled downward. 
>
> Lodged beside the long-stemmed bloom, the memory of your call cleaved to the roots unwinding down my neck. Rigid and unmoving, my body held tight and listened intently.

---

### Key Improvements Made:
* **Eliminated Choppy Sentence Fragments:** Smoothed out isolated transitional words (*"And."*, *"So."*, *"Only."*, *"Then."*) into elegant, connected sentences.
* **Elevated Vocabulary:** Refined phrases like *"crazed brain"* to *"frantic mind"* or *"tormented mind,"* and *"suckling"* to *"drawing life"* or *"feeding upon."*
* **Enhanced Rhythm:** Improved the cadence of the narrative to give the dark, surreal imagery a polished, poetic weight without changing any narrative events.

Had you summoned me, I would have rushed to your side, but my jaw was bound. A remarkably stunning, light-blush blossom was wedged tightly in my mouth, its thick stalk gripped fast between my teeth. Because its sharp barbs pierced deeply into the delicate, moist lining of my flesh, I was rendered completely incapable of vocalizing a response. 

Nevertheless, my lips shaped soundless messages toward you—expressions you could never hear. Inside my frantic mind, those thoughts roared with intense desperation, though they ultimately provided no help to you.

As time passed, the flower's delicate petals drooped, drifted away on the breeze, and decomposed into nutrient-rich soil within a stranger's garden. The tough, fibrous stalk grew dry and brittle. In an effort to break its hold, I clamped my jaws shut with force, but the immense pressure only caused my teeth to dislodge and fall out. By then, the prickers had embedded themselves permanently into my cheeks, actively feeding off my softest tissues. Shortly afterward, tiny green tendrils germinated from the rooted barbs, spiraling their way downward. 

The memory of your call remained anchored in my mind, resting side by side with the impression of that long-stemmed bloom. Both merged completely with the sprawling root network creeping down my neck, while my entire physical form froze in place, straining intently to listen.
outputs.L3:
When the phone began to ring, I was powerless to answer it. A thick, thorny rose stem was clenched tightly between my teeth, locking my jaw in place and sealing my silence. I tried desperately to call out, moving my lips into the shapes of words and screaming into the quiet room, but no sound could break past the wooden barrier. On the other end of the line, the caller listened to the empty air for a few agonizing moments before hanging up, entirely unaware of my frantic, silent response.

As time passed, the world kept moving, but the rose remained. One by one, its velvety petals withered, dried, and were carried away by the breeze, leaving behind only the bare, hardened stem. Desperate to free myself from its grasp, I tried to bite down with all my strength to shatter the wood. But the stem’s grip was unyielding; instead of breaking the branch, the force fractured my own teeth. They crumbled and fell away, leaving me completely surrendered to the plant's hold.

Deprived of my teeth, the rose did not die—it took hold. Its sharp thorns sank permanently into the soft tissue of my jaw, anchoring themselves into my flesh. Soon, the withered stem began to sprout new life, sending green shoots winding down the back of my throat. Day by day, the plant grew inward, pushing its dark roots deeper into my chest and weaving them around my organs until it became a permanent part of my anatomy. 

Now, the rose and I exist as one. Deep within my body, its root system continues to expand, heavy and inescapable. Yet, I no longer fight it. Instead, I carefully nurture the memory of that missed phone call, keeping the echoes of the unanswered ring safely preserved in the dark, quiet space where the roots have taken hold inside me.
outputs.L4:
The phone began to vibrate against the wooden grain of the bedside table, its low, rhythmic hum cutting through the suffocating stillness of the room. On the screen, a name flashed—a name that carried the weight of everything left unsaid, every unresolved grievance, and every tender truth I had spent months trying to bury. 

My chest tightened. The urge to reach out, to answer, to let my voice shatter the distance between us was almost violent. But terror, cold and absolute, paralyzed my hand. 

To keep myself from speaking—from letting even a single desperate sound escape my throat—I reached for the vase beside me. I pulled out a single pale pink rose. It was a deceptively delicate thing, its petals the soft color of dawn, but its stem was thick and armored with long, needle-sharp thorns. Without thinking, driven by a manic need to muzzle my own impulse, I shoved the stem horizontally into my mouth and bit down hard.

The thorns pierced the soft lining of my inner cheeks and punctured my tongue instantly. A metallic tang of blood filled my mouth, warm and thick, mingling with the bitter taste of crushed plant sap. Pain radiated through my jaw, but I pressed my teeth deeper into the wood of the stem, using the excruciating sting to anchor myself in place. *Do not answer,* I told myself. *Do not say a word.*

The phone rang and rang. Each vibration felt like a pulse beating directly against my exposed nerves. I stared at the screen, my breath coming in ragged, shallow gasps through my nose. With every swell of emotion, every urge to drop the barrier and cry out, I clenched my jaw tighter. The thorns sank deeper, embedding themselves in the muscle of my face. 

Eventually, the ringing stopped. The screen faded to black. The silence returned, heavier now, pregnant with the terminal finality of a missed connection. 

Yet, I could not unclench my teeth. Fear had locked my jaw; the pain had turned to numbness. Minutes bled into hours, and hours melted into a feverish, endless night. I lay there in the dark, a prisoner of my own making, holding the pale pink rose hostage between my lips.

As the days blended together in a haze of muted isolation, the rose began to change. Denied water, the flower did not simply die; it fed on me. The pale pink petals slowly browned and shriveled, falling like faded scales onto my chest, leaving behind only the raw, exposed receptacle. But while the blossom decayed, the stem found a dark, fertile nourishment in my blood and saliva.

It began with a subtle creeping sensation—a dull, itchy throbbing beneath my gums. The thorns that had punctured my flesh began to unfurl hidden, microscopic tendrils. Slowly, inexorably, the plant began to root. 

I felt the pale, fibrous shoots pushing their way down into the meat of my tongue, weaving around my jawbone, and anchoring themselves into the soft tissue of my palate. Small green vines burrowed under the skin of my neck, mapping out new, chlorophyll-laced veins beneath my throat. The pain ceased to be an external intrusion; it became my new anatomy. 

I tried once to pull it free, but the agony was blinding. The plant was no longer merely inside me; it was of me. To tear the stem from my teeth would mean tearing away my lower face, ripping out my vocal cords along with the tangled root system that now bound my throat in a permanent, thorny embrace.

Now, the pale pink rose is long gone, decayed into dust, but its living skeleton remains forever fused to my flesh. I carry the unspoken words like a calcified weight in my esophagus. My mouth is permanently held slightly ajar by the woody stem that lives inside my bones, ensuring that no word will ever pass my lips again. 

I am bound forever to that missed call, a living monument to cowardice. The silence I chose has become my body, proving that the things we refuse to say do not simply vanish into the air—they stay, they rot, and ultimately, they consume us from the inside out.

**When** the morning fog gently lifts over the slumbering valley, the world seems to reset itself. There is an unspoken promise in the silence of dawn, a brief moment where time feels momentarily suspended. As the sun creeps over the horizon, the forest slowly wakes, and every leaf holds a single drop of dew, shimmering bright as **its** delicate surface catches the first rays of light.

It is easy to remain comfortable in the stillness of where we are, hesitant to step into the noise and uncertainty of a new day. **But** growth rarely happens in static places. On the cold glass of the nightstand. 
You.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a gothic prose poem where the narrator explains why they couldn't respond to a loved one. Incorporate botanical body horror featuring a rose taking root inside the speaker's jaw, cheeks, and neck.
counterfactuals.output:
Do not think I abandoned you to the winter, my dearest, or that the silence stretching between our letters was a cruelty born of neglect. I did not speak, I did not call out your name across the darkening moors, because my voice was no longer mine to give; it had been harvested by a garden of dark velvet and bone.

It began as a splinter of sweet ache beneath my tongue—a seed drinking deeply from the subterranean moisture of my grief. Soon, the roots found the marrow of my jaw. They threaded through the hinge of my mandible, lacing tightly around bone until my mouth was anchored shut, a calcified, aching cage. I felt the slow, agonizing pulse of subterranean growth: tendrils creeping beneath the lining of my cheeks, stretching the skin translucent until my veins ran green with chlorophyll beneath a bruised, parchment pale. Petals unfurled against the inside of my flesh, soft and suffocating, pushing against my teeth like smooth river stones.

If I had parted my lips to answer your pleas, I would have torn my own face asunder.

Now, my neck is no longer a pillar for breath, but a wooden trellis. Thorns—black, curved, and needle-sharp—drag through the tender muscle of my throat, anchoring the heavy stem to the meat of my collarbones. When I attempt to swallow, I taste only the thick copper of my own blood mixed with the suffocating, sickly sweet attar of a dying bloom. A single crimson rose has filled the cavern of my mouth, its crushed velvet head resting heavy against my palate, strangling every word before it can reach the light.

So forgive my silence, my love. I could not write, I could not call to you from the shadows, for every phrase I wished to offer was strangled in the rich, damp soil of my own flesh—and when I tried to whisper that I was yours, I choked only on thorns.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Complete this story starter with a bizarre, dreamlike horror monologue: "I would have come. When you called. But..."
counterfactuals.output:
"I would have come. When you called. But...

...the floor had turned to warm, trembling grease, you see, and my ankles had forgotten their names. 

Do you know what happens when a phone rings inside a dream? Your voice didn't come through the speaker. It leaked out from behind the wallpaper, swelling in tiny, pale blisters that popped into salt and wet hair. I reached for the front door, but my hand—my good hand—had unspooled into six thin, chittering needles. I tried to tell them *stop*, but my tongue was just a velvet moth resting on a bed of dry ash.

And the hallway... oh, the hallway was so polite about it. It simply stretched itself into a throat and began to swallow its own light. 

I tried to put on my shoes. I really did. But the shoes were full of boiling milk. I stepped into them anyway because I wanted to reach you, but every step I took forward pushed me three inches backward into the plaster. The walls were eating my heels, sucking them down into the lath and horsehair with a low, wet sigh—a sound terribly like my grandmother trying to sing a lullaby backward.

I looked out the window to see if your car was there, but the glass didn't look outside anymore. It looked *inward*, right into the back of my own skull. I watched myself standing in the dark, trapped in a house that was slowly turning itself inside out. The ceiling became a floor of black soil, raining earthworms into my eyes, while the furniture began to breathe—in, out, in, out—matching the pulse of the dial tone.

By the time the third ring died, I wasn't a person at all. I was just a shape drawn in stale grease on the kitchen linoleum, listening to the ceiling fan slice through the moonlight. It cut the light into ribbons, you know? Cold, blue ribbons. 

I tried to tie them together so I could climb out to you. But they kept turning into fingers. Hundreds of tiny, damp fingers. All of them pointing at the wall. All of them whispering that you hadn't called me at all—that it was just the house, learning how to imitate your voice so I would stand still long enough for it to finish digesting me."
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a piece of poetic flash fiction about the painful physical cost of unspoken words? Use vivid, visceral imagery of thorns, falling teeth, wilting petals, and roots taking over a human body.
counterfactuals.output:
Silence is not empty; it is wet, heavy soil. 

It began behind my molars—a velvet weight that tasted of rust and rain. When you asked me what was wrong, the truth swelled in my throat, too jagged to pass, and so I swallowed it back down. 

That night, the taproot took.

It drank from my marrow, slow and greedy. By morning, my chest felt crowded, a dark greenhouse blooming beneath my sternum. Pale, fibrous tendrils wound around my ribcage, using my bones as a trellis, squeezing with every hesitant breath. I could hear them shifting inside me—a dry, rustling hiss of creeping ivy invading the dark hollows of my lungs.

By the third day, the pain sharpened. The unsent apologies and buried grievances matured into thick, black-green briers. Thorns, hard as bone and sharp as needles, tore through the delicate lining of my esophagus. Every swallowed drop of water was a razor blade; every exhaled breath dragged metal across raw flesh. I tried to cough, to purge the stifling growth, but my lungs only produced a spray of bruised, copper-stained violet petals—wilting before they hit the cold ceramic of the sink. 

They were beautiful words once, perhaps. But left in the dark, they had rotted. 

Then came the looseness in my jaw. I reached into my mouth and felt the sickening give of my own anatomy. My teeth, pushed from their bloody sockets by the relentless upward thrust of new stems, clattered one by one into my palm like hollow ivory seeds. In the red gaps they left behind, blunt green shoots broke through the gums, bitter and thirsty for the light. 

I stood before the mirror as the sun bled out over the horizon. I opened my mouth to scream your name, to finally vomit the suffocating garden out onto the floor, but no sound came. 

A single, blackened rosebud pushed past my lips, unfurling its dying petals over my tongue. Outside my skin, tiny thorned vines were already breaking through the pores of my throat, weaving my jaw shut with green thread. 

I looked down at my hands. Beneath the translucent skin of my wrists, dark roots pulsed in place of veins. The silence had taken everything, blooming triumphantly out of my flesh, leaving me a hollow vase for the heavy, beautiful horror of all we never said.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a surrealist monologue about silence, regret, and plant metamorphosis. The speaker should sound unhinged and obsessed with the rose that prevented them from speaking.
counterfactuals.output:
*(The speaker is crouched, clutching their throat, staring wide-eyed at a point just above the listener’s head. Their breath hitches with a wet, rustling sound, like dry leaves being crushed underwater.)*

Shh! Don’t breathe. If you breathe, the spores will catch the draft, and I can’t—I *can’t* let them drift again. 

Do you know what silence tastes like? It doesn’t taste like nothing. It tastes like copper and wet soil. It tastes like *her*. 

I had the words, you see. I had them lined up right behind my teeth, a gorgeous, screaming army of *I’m sorrys* and *please don’ts* and *stay, stay, stay*. I opened my mouth to let them out, to fix the world, but *she* was waiting. Right at the base of my tongue. 

The Rose. 

Not a flower, no, no, no—don't be naïve! A velvet padlock. A crimson parasite. A thief with petrified hips! 

The second I tried to speak, she uncurled a petal. Just one. Wet and heavy, smelling of bruised iron and stagnant rain. It pressed down on my throat. *“Hush,”* she didn’t say—she doesn’t have a voice, she *steals* voices—she just bloomed. One petal became three, three became twelve, a tight, suffocating fist of damask choking back my confession. I swallowed my apology, and do you know what happens when you swallow a word you were meant to say? It rots. It turns into nitrate. It turns into *fertilizer*.

She fed on it! She drank my cowardice and grew four inches by midnight!

Look—look at my wrists! Look under the skin! Do you see those blue lines? They aren’t veins anymore. They’re phloem. They’re xylem. They’re pumping chlorophyll through my heartbeat! Every time I think about that afternoon—about the way the light fell on the door as it slammed—a new thorn scrapes against the inside of my ribs. *Scritch, scritch, scritch.* 

I am a greenhouse for my own cowardice! 

My lungs are filling with mulch. Yesterday, I coughed up a sepal. A green, hairy sepal, coated in my own bile. My spine is hardening into wood—can't you hear the bark snapping when I bend? I am losing my knees to the carpet! I am taking root in this carpet! 

If I had just spoken... if I had just bitten through the petals and spat her out onto the linoleum, bloody and torn... but I didn't. I let her stay. I liked the smell at first. Oh, I was vain! I thought, *Look at me, I harbor beauty, I harbor silence.* But silence isn't peace! Silence is a quiet, hungry root wrapping around your hyoid bone until your jaw unhinges!

*(The speaker suddenly freezes, their eyes dilating. They gently touch their own mouth, trembling.)*

Oh. Oh, no. 

It’s happening again. She’s stretching. 

She wants the rest of me. She’s turning my esophagus into a trellis. Can you see it? The red is coming out of my eyes now. The petals are pushing behind my eyelids. I can't—I can't see you through the leaves. 

Don't look at me like that! Don't look at me with your clear, soft, meat-throat! 

*(Whispering, barely able to force the air out, sound muffled by imaginary foliage)*

If you see her... if you ever see the person I was supposed to speak to... tell them... tell them I couldn't say it because... because... 

*(The speaker’s mouth flies open in a silent scream. They snap their jaws shut, shaking violently, before slowly softening into a rigid, statue-like pose. They lower their voice to a terrifyingly serene, papery rustle.)*

...because the rose preferred the quiet. And the rose... is so... very... thirsty.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
